meta.description: Reference ranges, colour thresholds and plain-English guidance for the astronaut Daily Check-in (app.services.checkin_service). Every threshold carries its own source and status. Loaded at runtime; do not hardcode these values elsewhere.

status_definitions.literature: threshold stated in the cited source
status_definitions.assumed: no source found for this exact cut-off; project assumption, disclosed in the API response

meta.threshold_semantics: Each threshold is {color, direction, value, inclusive}. direction 'below': flagged when value < threshold (<= if inclusive). direction 'above': flagged when value > threshold (>= if inclusive). Red thresholds are checked before amber; otherwise green.
meta.disclaimer: Decision-support prototype, not a medical device.

AHA_ACC_BP_2025.citation: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology. 2025 AHA/ACC/multisociety Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults. Blood pressure categories unchanged from the 2017 guideline (Whelton PK et al., Hypertension 2018;71:e13-e115, doi:10.1161/HYP.0000000000000065): Normal <120 and <80; Elevated 120-129 and <80; Stage 1 130-139 or 80-89; Stage 2 >=140 or >=90 mmHg.
AHA_ACC_BP_2025.access: category cut-offs confirmed via guideline summaries (AHA professional 'Top things to know', Harvard Health); heart.org page not reachable from our build environment

MEDLINEPLUS_LOW_BP.citation: MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine). Low Blood Pressure: 'If your blood pressure reading is 90/60 or lower, you have low blood pressure.' Low readings matter mainly when they cause symptoms.

AHA_HEART_RATE.citation: American Heart Association. All About Heart Rate (Pulse): a resting heart rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute is normal for most adults; well-trained athletes can be lower.
AHA_HEART_RATE.access: via secondary sources quoting the AHA page (AARP, Fortune); heart.org not reachable from our build environment

ACC_AHA_HRS_BRADY_2018.citation: Kusumoto FM et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Heart Rhythm 2019;16(9):e128-e226 (also Circulation 2019;140:e382-e482). Sinus bradycardia: sinus rate <50 bpm; normal 50-100 bpm (ACC press release).
ACC_AHA_HRS_BRADY_2018.access: ACC 'Guidelines Made Simple' table and ACC press release; full guideline text not read

ADA_SOC_2026_DIAGNOSIS.citation: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 49(Suppl 1). Fasting plasma glucose 100-125 mg/dL = prediabetes; >=126 mg/dL = diabetes range (fasting = no caloric intake for >=8 h; diagnosis needs confirmation).
ADA_SOC_2026_DIAGNOSIS.access: thresholds confirmed via 2026 Standards summaries (PMC, Guideline Central); full section not read

ADA_HYPOGLYCEMIA_LEVELS.citation: International Hypoglycaemia Study Group. Glucose concentrations of less than 3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL) should be reported in clinical trials: a joint position statement of the ADA and EASD. Diabetes Care 2017;40(1):155-157. Adopted in ADA Standards of Care Section 6 (Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia): Level 1 <70 mg/dL, Level 2 <54 mg/dL.
ADA_HYPOGLYCEMIA_LEVELS.access: long-standing ADA classification; 2026 Section 6 text not re-read for this release

CDC_FEVER.citation: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Definitions of Signs, Symptoms, and Conditions of Ill Travelers: fever = measured temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or greater.

STATPEARLS_HYPOTHERMIA.citation: Hypothermia. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf NBK545239): hypothermia = core body temperature below 35 C (95 F); mild 32-35 C.

STAHN_2017.citation: Stahn AC et al. Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions. Scientific Reports 7:16180 (2017). Resting core body temperature rose by about 1 C on the ISS, developing over ~2.5 months.

NSF_SLEEP_2015.citation: Hirshkowitz M et al. National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary. Sleep Health 1(1):40-43 (2015). Adults 26-64: recommended 7-9 h; may be appropriate 6 h and 10 h; not recommended <6 h or >10 h.

NASA_HRP_HAZARDS.citation: NASA Human Research Program. The Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile/closed environments.
NASA_HRP_HAZARDS.access: search-result excerpts of the NASA page

MODEL_ASSUMPTION.citation: Assumption of this project (no source found for this exact cut-off).

routine.when: Every Sol, right after waking: before breakfast, coffee or exercise.
routine.why: Same time and conditions every Sol make today's numbers comparable with your own normal.

baseline.flag_abs_z_note: Same |z| >= 2 rule (WATCH_Z) as the Crew Health vitals channel (app.ml.anomaly).
baseline.sd_floor_note: Measurement-noise floors so a very steady history does not turn tiny changes into flags. heart_rate_bpm and sleep_hours match VITAL_SD_FLOOR in app.ml.physiology; the others are assumptions.

heart_rate.label: Resting heart rate
heart_rate.range_text: Green 50-100 bpm · Amber 40-49 or 101-120 · Red <40 or >120

heart_rate_bpm.where_in_source: Sinus bradycardia defined as sinus rate <50 bpm

guidance.how_to_measure: Sit still for 5 minutes after waking. Use the pulse sensor, or count beats at your wrist for 30 seconds and multiply by 2.
guidance.why_it_matters_in_space: Weightlessness (gravity hazard) de-conditions the heart and blood vessels; a resting pulse that drifts tells you early.

meaning.green: Your heart is beating at a normal resting pace.
meaning.amber_low: Your pulse is slower than usual for most adults. In fit people this can be normal, but watch for dizziness.
meaning.red_low: Your pulse is very slow. This can make you dizzy or faint.
meaning.amber_high: Your pulse is faster than normal for rest. Stress, poor sleep, caffeine, heat or dehydration can cause this.
meaning.red_high: Your resting pulse is very fast. Your body may be under strain (illness, dehydration, heart rhythm problem).

what_to_do.green: Nothing to do. Keep your exercise routine.
what_to_do.amber_low: Re-measure after 10 minutes of rest. If you feel dizzy or weak, stop exercise and tell a crewmate.
what_to_do.red_low: Sit or lie down, don't exercise, re-measure in 10 minutes and contact the flight surgeon.
what_to_do.amber_high: Drink water, rest 10 minutes, avoid caffeine and re-measure.
what_to_do.red_high: Stop all activity, sit down, drink water, re-measure in 10 minutes and contact the flight surgeon.

escalate_reason.red_low: Very slow resting heart rate: the flight surgeon should check heart rhythm.
escalate_reason.red_high: Very fast resting heart rate: the flight surgeon should check for illness, dehydration or rhythm problems.

guidance.how_to_measure: Sit 5 minutes, feet flat, cuff on bare upper arm at heart level. Don't talk. Take 2 readings 1 minute apart and enter the second.
guidance.why_it_matters_in_space: Without gravity (gravity hazard) body fluids shift to the head; blood pressure control changes and can fail when standing up again on Mars.

meaning.green: Your blood pressure is in the normal range.
meaning.amber_low: Your blood pressure is on the low side. Fine if you feel well; it can cause light-headedness when you stand up.
meaning.red_low: Your blood pressure is very low. You may faint, especially when moving or standing.
meaning.amber_high: Your blood pressure is above normal (elevated / stage 1). Stress, salt, poor sleep or fluid shifts can raise it.
meaning.red_high: Your blood pressure is high (stage 2 range). Over time this strains your heart and blood vessels.

what_to_do.amber_low: Drink water, stand up slowly, and re-measure. Tell a crewmate if you feel dizzy.
what_to_do.red_low: Lie down with legs raised, drink fluids, don't exercise, and contact the flight surgeon.
what_to_do.amber_high: Rest 5 minutes and re-measure. Cut salty snacks today and take a short relaxation break.
what_to_do.red_high: Rest 5 minutes and re-measure. If it is still this high, contact the flight surgeon.

escalate_reason.red_low: Very low blood pressure risks fainting: the flight surgeon should assess fluids and symptoms.
escalate_reason.red_high: Blood pressure in the stage 2 range: the flight surgeon should confirm and decide on treatment.

blood_glucose_mg_dl.where_in_source: Diabetes range: fasting plasma glucose >=126 mg/dL (needs confirmation)

guidance.how_to_measure: Before eating or drinking anything but water (8 h fast). Wash and dry your fingertip, prick the side, use the second drop on the meter strip.
guidance.why_it_matters_in_space: Inactivity, stress hormones and an altered diet in a closed habitat (closed-environment hazard) can disturb how your body handles sugar.

meaning.green: Your fasting blood sugar is normal.
meaning.amber_low: Your blood sugar is low. You may feel shaky, sweaty or unfocused.
meaning.red_low: Your blood sugar is dangerously low. This can quickly affect your thinking and safety.
meaning.amber_high: Your fasting blood sugar is above normal. Check that you really fasted; stress and poor sleep can also raise it.
meaning.red_high: Your fasting blood sugar is in the diabetes range. One reading is not a diagnosis, but it must be checked.

what_to_do.green: Nothing to do. Eat your planned breakfast.
what_to_do.amber_low: Eat or drink 15 g of fast sugar (juice, glucose tab), wait 15 minutes, re-measure.
what_to_do.red_low: Take 15 g of fast sugar now, tell a crewmate, re-measure in 15 minutes and contact the flight surgeon.
what_to_do.amber_high: Make sure you fasted 8 h, re-measure tomorrow, and keep to planned meals and exercise.
what_to_do.red_high: Re-measure fasting tomorrow and contact the flight surgeon with both readings.

escalate_reason.red_low: Level 2 hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) is a safety risk: the flight surgeon must be informed.
escalate_reason.red_high: Fasting glucose in the diabetes range: the flight surgeon should confirm and investigate.

body_temp_c.where_in_source: Upper green edge set with STAHN_2017 in mind: resting core temperature runs ~1 C higher on long missions, so a slightly raised reading alone is not red.

guidance.how_to_measure: Thermometer under the tongue, mouth closed, for the full beep. No hot or cold drinks for 15 minutes before.
guidance.why_it_matters_in_space: In a closed habitat (closed-environment hazard) infections spread easily and spaceflight weakens immunity; resting body temperature also runs ~1 °C higher on long missions.

meaning.amber_low: Your temperature is a bit low. Check the measurement; the habitat may be cold.
meaning.red_low: Your temperature is dangerously low (hypothermia range).
meaning.amber_high: Your temperature is slightly raised. Possible start of an infection, or heat after exercise.
meaning.red_high: You have a fever. Your body is likely fighting an infection, which can spread to the crew.

what_to_do.amber_low: Put on warm layers, have a warm drink, re-measure in 30 minutes.
what_to_do.red_low: Warm up now (layers, sleeping bag, warm drink), tell a crewmate and contact the flight surgeon.
what_to_do.amber_high: Rest, drink water and re-measure in 2 hours. Wash hands often.
what_to_do.red_high: Rest, drink water, limit close contact with the crew and contact the flight surgeon.

escalate_reason.red_low: Temperature in the hypothermia range: the flight surgeon must be informed.
escalate_reason.red_high: Fever (>=38.0 °C): the flight surgeon should assess infection risk for you and the crew.

sleep.label: Sleep last night
sleep.range_text: Green 7-9 h · Amber 6-6.9 or 9.1-10 h · Red <6 or >10 h

sleep_hours.where_in_source: Adults 26-64: recommended 7-9 h; 6 h may be appropriate
Adults 26-64: recommended 7-9 h; 10 h may be appropriate

guidance.how_to_measure: Count hours actually asleep (not time in the sleep bag). Use your sleep tracker if you wear one.
guidance.why_it_matters_in_space: No natural day/night, noise and confinement (isolation hazard) disrupt sleep; tired crew make more mistakes during critical tasks.

meaning.amber_low: You slept a bit less than recommended. Focus and mood can suffer today.
meaning.red_low: You slept far too little. Reaction time and judgement are clearly reduced.
meaning.amber_high: You slept longer than usual. Fine after a hard day, but a pattern can signal illness or low mood.
meaning.red_high: You slept a very long time. This can be a sign of illness, exhaustion or low mood.

what_to_do.green: Nothing to do. Keep the same sleep schedule.
what_to_do.amber_low: Avoid caffeine after midday, dim screens 1 h before sleep, keep the same bedtime tonight.
what_to_do.red_low: Avoid safety-critical tasks without a double-check today, plan a 20-minute nap and contact the flight surgeon if this repeats.
what_to_do.amber_high: Notice how you feel; get some light and exercise early in the day.
what_to_do.red_high: Check for fever or feeling unwell and contact the flight surgeon.

escalate_reason.red_low: Less than 6 h sleep impairs performance: the flight surgeon can adjust the schedule or lighting.
escalate_reason.red_high: More than 10 h sleep can signal illness or depression: the flight surgeon should check in.

guidance.how_to_measure: Pick the face that best matches how you have felt since waking: 1 = very low, 3 = okay, 5 = great.
guidance.why_it_matters_in_space: Months of isolation and confinement far from Earth (isolation and distance hazards) wear down mood and team cohesion.

meaning.green: Your mood is okay or good.

what_to_do.amber_low: Do something you enjoy, talk to a crewmate, schedule a private call home.
what_to_do.red_low: Talk to a crewmate you trust and contact the flight surgeon or behavioral-health support today.

escalate_reason.red_low: Very low mood: the flight surgeon / behavioral-health team should check in confidentially.
